title: TimescaleDB & Time-Series Engineering
description: Process billions of IoT metrics and stock ticks using Hypertables, automatic chunk partitioning, and continuous aggregates.

data.text: **TimescaleDB** is an extension that transforms PostgreSQL into a high-performance time-series database. It abstracts complex table partitioning behind **Hypertables**, automatically splitting data into time chunks without user intervention.

data.title: Creating a Hypertable with Continuous Aggregation
data.content: Automates downsampling of raw sensor readings into hourly rollups.
data.code:
-- 1. Create standard table
CREATE TABLE sensor_readings (
    recorded_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    device_id INT NOT NULL,
    cpu_temp NUMERIC,
    battery_pct NUMERIC
);

-- 2. Convert into TimescaleDB Hypertable partitioned by 7-day chunks
SELECT create_hypertable('sensor_readings', 'recorded_at', chunk_time_interval => INTERVAL '7 days');

-- 3. Fast time-bucket aggregation
SELECT 
    time_bucket('1 hour', recorded_at) AS hour_bucket,
    device_id,
    AVG(cpu_temp) AS avg_temp
FROM sensor_readings
WHERE recorded_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '24 hours'
GROUP BY hour_bucket, device_id
ORDER BY hour_bucket DESC;

data.text: A continuous aggregate is a materialized view that TimescaleDB keeps refreshed incrementally over time buckets, so dashboards read pre-aggregated data instead of scanning raw rows. A retention policy drops old chunks, and chunks make that a fast metadata operation rather than a huge delete.

data.title: Bucket readings into hourly rollups and drop old data
data.content: The continuous aggregate materializes hourly averages; the retention policy keeps two years of raw data.
data.code:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW readings_hourly
WITH (timescaledb.continuous) AS
SELECT
    time_bucket('1 hour', recorded_at) AS bucket,
    sensor_id,
    avg(temperature) AS avg_temp,
    max(temperature) AS max_temp
FROM readings
GROUP BY bucket, sensor_id;

-- Refresh automatically as new data arrives
SELECT add_continuous_aggregate_policy('readings_hourly',
    start_offset => INTERVAL '3 hours',
    end_offset   => INTERVAL '1 hour',
    schedule_interval => INTERVAL '1 hour');

-- Drop raw chunks older than two years
SELECT add_retention_policy('readings', INTERVAL '2 years');

data.title: Interview angle: time-series data wants chunking, not one giant table
data.text: A time-series workload writes constantly and queries recent data far more than old data. Chunking by time keeps the hot chunks small enough to stay in cache, makes retention a metadata drop instead of a mass delete, and lets an index cover only recent data. TimescaleDB automates that, but the underlying idea — partition by time, drop whole partitions to expire data — is exactly what you would build by hand with declarative partitioning.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: TimescaleDB provides automatic chunk partitioning via Hypertables.
Delivers 10x-100x faster time-series analytical queries than vanilla PostgreSQL.
`time_bucket()` simplifies grouping metrics into arbitrary intervals (15m, 1h, 1d).
